implementation_notes: There is no JavaScript prefetch instruction and there could not be: the runtime abstracts the machine. The only deliberate prefetch a JavaScript program can issue is a network-level one - fetch(url, {priority: 'high'}) on the Chromium network stack, preload/prefetch resource hints in HTML, or a Worker starting its own work early so its JIT warms and its data loads while the main thread is busy. For CPU memory, the entire lever is data locality: typed arrays (Float64Array) are contiguous and outside the JS heap's object graph, so a numeric loop over a typed array is the JavaScript analogue of a prefetchable, streaming access pattern. Without a typed array, an array of objects is a pointer chase. The event loop itself already overlaps I/O with compute, so the dominant JS latency is network and main-thread jank rather than cache misses.
idiom_name: no CPU prefetch; use typed arrays for locality, fetch priority / preload for network prefetch, and Workers to overlap startup
pitfalls: There is no CPU prefetch in JavaScript; a loop over an array of objects is a pointer chase that a typed array avoids.
fetch({priority:'high'}) is a Chromium-only hint and is ignored elsewhere; it is not a guarantee of ordering.
preload/prefetch resource hints can waste bandwidth if the resource is not actually used next.
The dominant JS latency is main-thread jank and network, not cache misses - prefetching the network or moving work to a Worker usually beats any CPU-level hint.
